questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: That the university offered courses on documentation of endagered languages. The choice of Victoria also came about because I had friends there.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: My stay was super great, but at times the workload from UVic was too much and I got stressed. Sometimes, this meant that I would spend my weekends working instead of going out and exploring the area.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy. The exchange coordinators sent out plenty of e-mails to prepare us for our stay, also informing us where we could find additional information.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: UVic's exchange coordinators hosted many meetings upon arrival to introduce us to many aspects of UVic life. The instructors and students were also very helpful in answering my questions on studying in Canada.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I heard it was quite difficult for many people, who didn't have luck with neither on-campus allotment nor housing Facebook groups. I had my personal connections, so it was easy for me. I would suggest that you put your eggs in many different baskets; the university's on-campus housing options, facebook groups, and airbnb.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: You may not get as close to the other exchange students that live on campus since they do everyday stuff together, while you may have a longer commute to get to campus. In that avenue, it is definitely worth it to get a public transit pass. You do also have a better chance, in my opinion, to really experience the local culture.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The students living on-campus were very young because housing is mostly offered to first year students (18-ish years old), and that is why I opted to live off-campus. Also, the housing rules were absurdly strict.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The process was mostly transparent, and the exchange coordinators sent e-mails with very detailed instructions, which was very much appreciated.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
You get a list with courses that are recommended for exchange students, and you can also look on the website for additional courses if you wish. Before registration opens, you may have to submit information on prior courses if the course you want to take has prerequisites. The coordinators are quick to let you know whether or not you can get into the course, and if the course is open at all.
Then you get a time slot allotted for some time around May, and at that time, you can begin registering for courses. You go into the university's website (where you have to make an account), and then you search for the courses. Then you see if there are any vacant spots on the course, and then you register. If it is full, you can stand in line and wait for someone to deselect the course.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The exchange coordinators sent e-mails with thorough instructions on how to register for courses and information on what courses were suggested. They were also quick to answer questions.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got into all the courses I selected from the list of suggested courses. However, many of the courses I had seen in the university's course catalogue were not offered that term, unfortunately.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Do it early! And try to find information in the course catalogue on whether or not the course will be offered in your term.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I found it to be very interesting, going into niche fields and using other methodologies than I was used to. However, I found the academic level to be somewhat lower and the workload to be too high.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: They were not as challenging as what I have been used to at UCPH.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
In general, there was more lecturing, with instructors just repeating the content of the assigned readings, and less room for questions and discussions. When there were discussions, they were also more about personal opinion and social/political issues, whereas at UCPH I remember it being more academic. One course, however, (LING 387: Task-based language teaching) had it very opposite, where students presented and experimented with planned lessons most of the time. This course also had extreme enthusiasm and activity based learning.
Furthermore, tests were more about remembering facts than applying methodologies than what I remember from UCPH.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
IS 101 - Indigenous Studies Foundations
LING/PSYC 370 B - Child Language Acquisition
LING 387 - Task-based language teaching
LING 431 - Community-based language revitalization

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
IS 101 was super fascinating, since I learned about a side of Canada that I would probably not have heard about otherwise. Also, it helped me develop a new outlook on life, realizing how cultures can be different and how people relate to each other and the world.
The instructor in LING 387 was extremely enthusiastic, and her methods of teaching helped me learn a lot. She provides food every lesson and creates a very friendly atmosphere, so it is a good time. There is a lot of work, but the rewards are definitely tangible.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: The study permit did cost more than I expected, especially because I needed my fingerprints scanned, which I had to go to Stockholm to do - the other closest option was in Germany.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
I thought groceries would be cheaper than in Denmark, but they were just as expensive - Walmart was pretty much the only affordable supermarket. UVic, however, did have a food bank where you could get free food once a week, which helped a lot.
Phone data plans were quite expensive.
Transportation with bus and ferry was cheaper than I had expected.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I did not join any clubs, but facilities were pretty nice, and the clubs sure did look interesting.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Sports clubs, a caving club, dance classes, color run (combined with Holi), karaoke nights, pub quiz, etc.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Karaoke night, pub quiz, color run, the caving club

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go to nature, there are many great spots to visit all around. In the city, I would recommend the game arcade, board game cafes, the Beacon Hill park, the Royal B.C. museum, the harbour, Mount Douglas.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was pretty easy, it was not too different from the Danish culture.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Just talk to them, they are usually quite willing to get to know you. Ask them about Canada, or tell them about Europe, I had good succes with that.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Sometimes, I found it hard to give constructive criticism. It seems that Canadians prefer positivity and avoid anything resembling negativity, so they will add a lot of positives when giving feedback. Also, sometimes I found this focus on positivity and being upbeat annoying if the situation didn't call for it. Furthermore, personal opinions were shared quite intensely, which I wasn't used to.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The willingness to talk to strangers and the thankfulness the Canadians showed (they would say 'thank you' after lessons and when going off the bus). I also appreciate how much people in Victoria go on hikes in nature. Also, the population here is very diverse, so you get to see many cultures co-exist.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Use the UVSS food hamper, it will save you a lot of money.
2) Bring your hiking boots, and don't forget your rain jacket.
3) Especially if you live on-campus, remember to get out and see the city of Victoria!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be prepared to do a lot of work. Get started soon so it doesn't all pile up and become unbearable.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting many different people with interesting stories to tell. Experiencing breath-taking nature. Changing my outlook on life and gaining confidence by being self-sufficient.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The workload for sure.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: No =)

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
